Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The place is Juniper Row, a fictional neighborhood on the east side of Bellwether. The station sits on the roof of the Juniper Row library annex, not the main library building. It was installed in 2018 by residents who wanted local readings because the official airport station is several miles away and often misses the differences between the river blocks and the hill streets. A volunteer group called the Juniper Row Weather Circle checks it. There are seven regular volunteers, but don't make it sound like all seven are always working together. The station measures air temperature, rainfall, wind speed and wind direction. It doesn't predict the weather, and it isn't a warning system. Use October 14 as the date of the episode, during a fall rainstorm. Rain started before dawn, and by 5:10 a.m. the station's rain gauge had recorded 18 millimeters. A wind gust of 41 kilometers per hour was recorded at 5:55 a.m. At 6:20 a.m. the online readings stopped updating. Don't say that the entire station failed: the temperature and wind instruments were still running, but the rain gauge data stopped reaching the online display because a cable connector had become wet. At 6:30, volunteer Marta Ruiz took a temperature reading of 9.8 degrees Celsius from the station's separate display and wrote it in the paper log. The online gap should be clear without implying that there was no information at all. I don't know the total rainfall for the whole day, so don't supply one or suggest the early figure was the storm total.

Marta was at the annex that morning with volunteer Dev Patel. Dev had brought a thermos and was trying to keep the paper log from getting damp. Marta looked at the connection and said, “The gauge didn't fail; the cable was soaked.” Please use that as an ordinary reported quote, not a big dramatic reveal, and don't change her words. Around 7:00 a.m. the rain was still coming down, and the two volunteers put a plastic cover over the logbook while they waited for the display to refresh. The station was still visible from the library courtyard, though there were no visitors there yet. Don't add a rescue, emergency call, dangerous flooding, or a crowd watching them. This is a modest local incident.

A few neighbors noticed the missing online readings later that morning. Inez Cole, who lives on the river side of Juniper Row, normally checks the station before walking her dog, and she sent a message to the Weather Circle asking whether the quiet display meant it had stopped raining. Don't answer that question on her behalf or make her claim she relied on the gauge for safety. She only wanted to know why the page had gone blank. Tomas Bell, who runs the corner grocery on Hill Street, checks wind direction before putting out his sidewalk chalkboard. He said the airport report was useful but didn't always describe the wind on his street. Keep those as small examples of why local measurements interest people, not proof that this station is more accurate in every situation.

It would be helpful to have a short numbered section in the feature, perhaps a small reading timeline that readers can scan. Use these entries and keep their times and units exact: 1. 5:10 a.m. — 18 millimeters of rain recorded; 2. 5:55 a.m. — a 41-kilometer-per-hour wind gust recorded; 3. 6:20 a.m. — online rain gauge updates stopped; 4. 6:30 a.m. — Marta logged a temperature of 9.8 degrees Celsius from the separate display. The display gap doesn't mean the temperature reading vanished, and the time sequence shouldn't be rearranged to make it sound like it all happened at once. The feature can explain that one measurement was still available on site even though the rain-gauge reading was no longer appearing online.

For background, the paper log is kept in a blue binder in a cabinet inside the annex. Volunteers enter readings there when they visit, and sometimes copy observations from the station display if the online page is lagging. The Weather Circle posts the online readings for neighbors, but its members don't promise round-the-clock monitoring. Marta and Dev didn't have a repair kit with them on October 14. At 8:15 a.m. the rain-gauge feed was still missing from the online page, and Dev wrote that the connector needed to dry before they could test it. Keep the repair status at that point: don't invent when service resumed, whether a replacement was installed, or whether the whole day’s log was later completed. The library annex remained open as usual; the storm did not close it.

Please make the final paragraph give distinct information rather than repeat the storm timeline or wrap up with a general lesson. It can mention the Weather Circle’s next scheduled check, which is October 19, when volunteers plan to compare the paper log with the online readings and inspect the connector if it is dry. That is a plan, not a report that the check has already happened.
